title: The lopsided begonia leaf reflects unequal, not asymmetrical, growth

fields.label: Label
fields.value: The lopsided begonia leaf reflects unequal, not asymmetrical, growth

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: The two halves of a begonia leaf, one ovate and the other cordate, are mathematically similar figures produced by unequal growth on either side of the midrib, so that angles to equal radii on the two sides are in constant proportion.

fields.label: Notation
fields.value: \theta' = k\theta for angles to equal radii on the two halves of the leaf

fields.label: Chapter
fields.value: Ch. XVII: On the Theory of Transformations, or the Comparison of Related Forms

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: the so-called unsymmetrical leaf of a begonia, in which one side of the leaf may be merely ovate while the other has a cordate outline, is seen to be really a case of _unequal_, and not truly asymmetrical, growth on either side of the midrib.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci On Growth and Form claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: D’Arcy Wentworth Thompson, On Growth and Form (1st ed., Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1917), Chapter XVII, “On the Theory of Transformations, or the Comparison of Related Forms”; topic “Radial co-ordinates and leaf shape”. Scope: asymmetrical leaves of Begonia

fields.label: Notation
fields.value: \theta' = k\theta for angles to equal radii on the two halves of the leaf

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on thompson1917-ch17-08: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.75

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The constant-proportion geometric prediction is direct and can be evaluated on abundant digitized specimens. Data resolve mature shape well, but not the causal claim that unequal growth generated it.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Digitize corresponding radial landmarks on both sides of Begonia leaves and test whether a constant angular/radial mapping converts one half to the other with low residual error relative to unrestricted asymmetry models.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Herbarium images may be folded or lack developmental stage.

Mathematical similarity of mature halves does not establish growth dynamics.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:

discriminating power: 0.8
operationalizability: 0.9
data adequacy: 0.55

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The constant-proportion prediction is a simple measurement on leaf images, and Begonia is widely digitized. A varying angle ratio is a direct refutation, and a stable ratio across many leaves is positive evidence. Mounting distortion is a real bias and can be checked by comparing pressed sheets with photographs of fresh leaves in the same portal.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: On begonia leaves, measure angles from the base to corresponding radii on each side of the midrib and test whether those angles stay in a constant ratio. A stable ratio, mapping an ovate half onto a cordate half, would support unequal similar growth; a ratio that changes along the midrib would show true asymmetry and refute the claim.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Pressing and mounting distort angles, especially in thin cordate lobes.

Species and leaf position on the plant add biological scatter around a single ratio.
